hook: Latimer trained as a drilling and completion engineer at BHP Billiton before pairing an energy-track master's degree with an MBA at Stanford, then founded Fervo Energy, the enhanced-geothermal company applying oil-and-gas drilling techniques to clean baseload power. He has led the company for nearly nine years and was named a Presidential Leadership Scholar in 2022.
name: Tim Latimer

reading.body:
Tim Latimer's career is built on a single transferable insight: the horizontal drilling techniques that unlocked shale oil and gas can be redirected to extract clean, firm baseload power from geothermal heat.

His path from BHP Billiton's drilling operations to Stanford's joint energy and business program to founding Fervo Energy in 2017 is internally consistent in a way that matters. The oil and gas industry spent decades refining directional drilling at scale. Latimer carried that operational knowledge into a domain, enhanced geothermal systems, that had long been constrained by the inability to create reliable underground flow at commercial rates. The connection between his BHP years and Fervo's technical approach is not incidental; it is the founding premise.

For AI infrastructure, this matters because geothermal, if it can be commercialized broadly, offers something most clean energy sources do not: power that runs continuously regardless of weather, at sites that can in principle be located near load. Data centers require firm, around-the-clock electricity, and that requirement is one of the primary constraints on where and how fast AI compute can expand. The data here covers Latimer's background and Fervo's founding logic but does not speak to the company's current capacity, project pipeline, or whether its costs are competitive with other firm power sources. Those questions determine whether the approach scales from promising to consequential.
